meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'up with which I will not put'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous joke from a 1941 Sussex newspaper about an unnamed English master. Churchill's name was attached two years later; 'bloody nonsense' is a later embellishment.

answer.label: Not Churchill — an anonymous 1941 newspaper joke
answer.sourceLine: The joke first appears in The West Sussex Gazette on 31 July 1941, told about an unnamed high-school English master — no Churchill, and no ‘bloody.’ The punchline was simply “a thing up with which I will not put.” Churchill’s name was first attached to it in October 1943, and the version quoted today accumulated its embellishments after that.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: …a thing up with which I will not put.
trail: The oldest known appearance is The West Sussex Gazette, 31 July 1941: an anonymous joke about an unnamed English master correcting a pupil, with the punchline ‘a thing up with which I will not put.’ No Churchill, no expletive Quote Investigator ↗.

In May 1942 The Strand Magazine retold it under the title ‘The End of a Sentence,’ now set in a government department. Only on 9 October 1943 does a Nottingham newspaper tag the punchline ‘W.S.C.’ — the first Churchill connection, two years after the joke was already in print antedating thread ↗.
Linguists who have examined it regard the attribution as spurious — and note the further irony that the ‘rule’ the joke mocks was never a rule Churchill campaigned against Language Log ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1941 punchline in full. Everything people love about the modern version — ‘bloody nonsense,’ the imperious tone, Churchill himself — was added over the following five years.
source.rightsNote: Free to use. The joke is anonymous, first printed in a 1941 British newspaper, and a punchline of this length is not protectable by copyright in any case; there is no rights holder to clear. As with the other Churchill red herrings, the only real exposure is the credit line — do not print it over his name on something you sell. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill won the Nobel Prize in Literature and was famously exacting about prose — he really did send memoranda demanding brevity and plain English. That reputation is exactly what made him the natural host for a joke about pedantic grammar-correction, and it is why the anonymous 1941 version was, within two years, being told about him instead.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a rare case where the whole life of a misattribution is documented in dated newspapers: the joke, the drift, the moment a name gets attached, and the embellishments that follow.

items.why: The joke is in print in July 1941 about an unnamed schoolmaster. Churchill’s initials are first attached in October 1943 — two years later, and to a story that already existed without him chain ↗.

The 1941 punchline is plain: ‘a thing up with which I will not put.’ ‘This is the sort of bloody nonsense,’ ‘errant pedantry’ and the rest are decorations added as the story travelled — they make it sound more like Churchill, which is the point.

The joke lampoons a prohibition on ending sentences with prepositions that was never a real rule of English. So a fake quotation is used to ridicule a fake rule — and is quoted approvingly by people making a valid point about grammar Language Log ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Author unknown. First printed 31 July 1941 in The West Sussex Gazette, about an unnamed English master; Churchill’s name was attached in October 1943 full chain ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The joke works by obeying the rule so violently that the sentence collapses — you cannot avoid a stranded preposition here without producing gibberish, which is the argument. It is a genuinely good piece of grammatical satire, whoever wrote it.
Attaching it to Churchill improves the performance rather than the point. A prime minister scrawling it in a margin is funnier than a schoolmaster saying it, so that is the version that survived.
detailsBody: 31 July 1941, West Sussex Gazette: an unnamed English master — ‘a thing up with which I will not put.’
May 1942, The Strand Magazine: retitled ‘The End of a Sentence,’ now set in a government department.
9 October 1943, Nottingham newspaper: the punchline is tagged ‘W.S.C.’ for the first time.
1946, Washington Post: the fully Churchillized anecdote, embellishments and all.
context.pull: The joke was already two years old before anyone thought of Churchill.
